chunks: What bare-metal programming is. The question: What is bare-metal programming?
Bare-metal programming means writing firmware that runs directly on the chip with no operating system. Your code is the only software there.
After reset, startup code prepares memory and calls main . Your code then sets up the clock and peripherals by writing to their registers.
It runs an endless main loop, and interrupt handlers deal with urgent events.
Imagine a one-person shop. You do every job yourself, serving customers one after another in a loop.
A doorbell rings when someone urgent arrives, and you drop what you are doing, deal with it quickly, and go back. Nobody manages your time but you.
That gives you total control and no overhead, but if you spend a long time on one customer, everyone else waits.
Everything before main is startup code; after main , execution alternates between the background loop and interrupt handlers. There is no scheduler anywhere in this picture.
Super-loop: the endless main loop that does the background work. ISR: ("What an ISR is"): an interrupt service routine, the short handler that deals with urgent events.
Startup code: code that runs between reset and main , setting up memory. Register: ("What registers are"): a storage spot that controls a peripheral.
Bare-metal code writes to these directly. Non-blocking: checking for something and moving on, instead of waiting for it.
You want to blink an LED every 500 milliseconds and also handle bytes arriving on a serial port.
A blocking delay(500) would freeze the program for half a second, so incoming bytes would be missed or handled late. Instead, each time around the loop you check two things.
Has 500 milliseconds passed since the last blink? If so, toggle the LED. Has a byte arrived? If so, handle it. Neither check waits, so both jobs keep running.
"Bare-metal means firmware running directly on the hardware with no operating system.
After reset, startup code initialises memory and calls main, which configures clocks and peripherals via registers and then runs a super-loop, with interrupts handling urgent events.
It gives minimal overhead, full control and low power, but I must handle scheduling, drivers and concurrency myself, which gets harder as the system grows."
